nameStory: Woodland tobacco gets its name from its preference for naturalized woodland gardens and its membership in the tobacco genus. Unlike its famous cousin used for smoking, this South American native earned the 'woodland' part of its name because it thrives in partially shaded, forest-like settings rather than full sun tobacco fields.
description: Woodland tobacco is a tall, dramatic flowering plant that can reach 4-5 feet high, making it hard to miss in the garden. This South American native produces large, paddle-shaped leaves and stunning clusters of long, white tubular flowers that dangle gracefully from the stems. Though it's called tobacco, this is primarily grown as an ornamental plant for its impressive nighttime fragrance and striking appearance. It's a short-lived perennial or biennial that occasionally escapes cultivation in New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Long, narrow white trumpet-shaped flowers hang in drooping clusters, each bloom about 3-4 inches long with a sweet, intense fragrance that's strongest at night

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very large, soft paddle-shaped leaves up to 2 feet long that feel slightly sticky and fuzzy to the touch, arranged alternately up the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, sturdy plant reaching 4-5 feet with thick, upright stems and a somewhat tropical appearance

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small oval seed capsules that split open to release tiny dark seeds, developing after the flowers fade

habitat: Rarely found wild in New England, but occasionally escapes from gardens into disturbed areas near homes, roadsides, or woodland edges. Prefers rich, moist soil in partially shaded locations. Most commonly spotted in naturalized garden settings or abandoned homesteads where it was once cultivated.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as rosettes of large, soft leaves close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: Tall flowering stems develop and the spectacular white trumpet flowers bloom from mid to late summer, filling evening air with fragrance.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, plants begin to die back after first frost.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die completely, leaving only seeds that may germinate the following year.

funFact: Woodland tobacco flowers are perfectly timed for moth romance - they open and release their strongest perfume at dusk, specifically to attract sphinx moths with their incredibly long tongues that can reach deep into the 4-inch flower tubes!
confusionNotes: The enormous paddle-shaped leaves and drooping white trumpet flowers make this plant quite distinctive and unlikely to be confused with native species. However, the large leaves might remind some of burdock, but burdock has completely different purple thistle-like flowers.
contextualKnowledge: Though called tobacco and related to smoking tobacco, woodland tobacco contains different alkaloid compounds and has never been used commercially for smoking. It's part of the nightshade family, which also includes tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes - plants that often have similar star-shaped or tubular flowers.
compareHints: Woodland tobacco is much taller and more dramatic than its cousin jasmine tobacco, with longer flower tubes and larger leaves. While jasmine tobacco has upward-facing flowers in various colors, woodland tobacco's pure white blooms hang downward in elegant clusters. Aztec tobacco is much smaller and bushier with tiny yellow-green flowers, making woodland tobacco the giant of the tobacco family in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Jasmine tobacco is much more delicate and ornamental than its cousin woodland tobacco, which grows much taller (up to 10 feet) with smaller white flowers.
Aztec tobacco is much more compact and stocky than woodland tobacco, which grows 4-5 feet tall with larger white flowers.
